extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants, attorneys, agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on drafting and examining patent claim numerical ranges and amount limitations under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (definiteness). Covers when ranges, open-ended amounts, preference language, and phrases like 'effective amount' are definite or indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recitation of specific numerical ranges generally not indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, the recitation of specific numerical ranges in a claim does not raise an issue of whether a claim is definite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere presence of numerical ranges in a claim is not by itself a basis for a 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection. Examiners should look to whether the claim's boundaries are discernible rather than treating numeric ranges as presumptively indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow and broader ranges in the same claim can render claim indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a narrow numerical range that falls within a broader range in the same claim may render the claim indefinite when the boundaries of the claim are not discernible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Description of examples and preferences belongs in the specification rather than in a single claim. If it's unclear whether the narrower range is a limitation or merely an example/preference, make a 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection. Examiner should analyze whether the metes and bounds of the claim are clearly set forth. Examples of problematic language: (A) "a temperature of between 45 and 78 degrees Celsius, preferably between 50 and 60 degrees Celsius"; (B) "a predetermined quantity, for example, the maximum capacity."

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer narrower-range limitations in dependent claims or separate independent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting a narrower range in a dependent claim (or another independent claim) is proper even if it falls within the broader range of the parent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dependent claim that sets forth a narrower range than its parent should not be rejected as indefinite merely because it falls within the parent's broader range. Example: claim 1 recites "resistance is 70-150 ohms" and claim 2 recites "resistance is 70-100 ohms" — claim 2 should not be rejected as indefinite for that reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-ended numerical ranges require careful definiteness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Open-ended numerical ranges (e.g., "at least 20%") should be carefully analyzed for definiteness, particularly when dependent claims or other claim language appear to exclude the open-ended element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example caution: an independent claim recites "at least 20% sodium" while a dependent claim sets specific amounts of non-sodium ingredients adding to 100%, creating an ambiguity as to the 'at least' limitation unless percentages are expressly based on the weight of nonsodium ingredients. Examiners must resolve whether the claim language and specification make the scope clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical/impossible compositions do not automatically render claims indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that, in theory, could read on compositions impossible to formulate are not necessarily indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court held that a composition claimed as 20-80% A, 20-80% B and 1-25% C was not indefinite merely because some combinations would total more than 100% (In re Kroekel). Subject matter that cannot exist in fact cannot anticipate or infringe, but that theoretical impossibility does not alone make the claim indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum-only amount limits can be definite in context
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation specifying only a maximum amount (e.g., "maintained at less than 7 mole percent") does not automatically render a claim indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is clearly directed to a process or context where an upper limit makes sense, the absence of an explicit minimum does not necessarily mandate rejecting the claim as indefinite. Example: In re Kirsch held that imposing a maximum limit without a minimum does not require distorting the claim to preclude performance of the claimed process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meanings of certain open-ended phrases have been judicially defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Some common phrases have been given specific meanings in reported cases (e.g., 'up to' and 'not more than X% by weight').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law: 'up to' includes zero as a lower limit (In re Mochel); 'a moisture content of not more than 70% by weight' can be read on dry material (Ex parte Khusid). Examiners and drafters should be aware of these interpretations when assessing or drafting claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Effective amount" requires assessment of disclosure support and function
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'an effective amount' may or may not be indefinite; the proper test is whether one skilled in the art could determine specific values for the amount based on the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the amount is not critical and the written disclosure (including examples) enables a skilled artisan to determine what is effective, the phrase can be definite (In re Halleck). Conversely, 'an effective amount' is indefinite if the claim fails to state the function to be achieved and more than one effect can be implied (In re Fredericksen). Recent decisions trend toward accepting 'effective amount' when read in light of supporting disclosure and absent prior art introducing uncertainty (Ex parte Skuballa). Examiners should consider whether the specification gives guidelines or intended utilities that permit determination of effective amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure: apply 35 U.S.C. 112(b) when claim boundaries are unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is not clear whether a particular numerical expression is a claim limitation or merely an example/preference, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph) should be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should analyze the claim language and the specification to determine whether metes and bounds are set forth. Use case examples and the context of the disclosure to decide whether a limitation is definite; if not, issue a 112(b) rejection.
